# AI Native Software Engineering Workshop — Full Text

> A full-day interactive workshop teaching software developers how to work effectively with AI tools. Covers everything from LLM fundamentals to capability-first agentic workflows across Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, and Devin Desktop. Built and presented by Jan De Dobbeleer (Engineering Leader & Open Source Innovator).

**URL:** https://ainativedev.itdepends.be/
**Source:** https://github.com/JanDeDobbeleer/workshop_ai_native

**Audience:** Software developers of all levels. No prior AI experience required — comfortable with software development is enough.

**Format:** Full-day, instructor-led, hands-on. Delivered as a web-based interactive slideshow. Navigation is sequential (slide by slide) with the ability to jump to any section.

---

## Section: Introduction

Workshop overview and the AI-native developer mindset. Covers the "quantum state" of AI adoption — how developers simultaneously exist across multiple adoption stages of the technology lifecycle, rather than moving through them sequentially. Introduces the 4D Fluency Framework and three AI interaction modes.

## Section: LLMs (Large Language Models)

How large language models actually work. Topics: transformer architecture, tokenisation, context windows, attention mechanisms, hallucinations and their causes, GPU acceleration, and the difference between base models and instruction-tuned models. Understanding these fundamentals helps developers set correct expectations and use models more effectively.

## Section: AI Fluency

The 4D framework for effective AI collaboration:
- **Delegation** — deciding when and how to engage AI; knowing which tasks benefit from AI and which don't
- **Description** — communicating goals clearly; writing effective prompts; providing the right context
- **Discernment** — evaluating AI outputs critically; knowing when to trust, verify, or discard suggestions
- **Diligence** — taking responsibility for AI-assisted work; reviewing, testing, and owning what AI produces

Three interaction modes:
- **Augmentation** — human and AI collaborate interactively; human remains in the loop at every step
- **Automation** — AI executes specific, well-defined tasks autonomously; human reviews output
- **Agency** — AI acts independently on future tasks; human defines goals and approves outcomes

## Section: Prompting

The art of communicating with AI. Topics: prompt engineering patterns, chain-of-thought prompting, few-shot examples, zero-shot vs few-shot, role prompting, structured output, and avoiding common mistakes. Practical exercises with real-world coding scenarios.

## Section: Models

Choosing the right model for the job. Topics: the current model landscape (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, etc.), capability vs cost tradeoffs, reasoning models vs standard models, context window sizes, multimodal capabilities, and decision framework for model selection. Pro Tool Stack principle: cheap/repetitive tasks → fast local models; complex reasoning → frontier cloud; sensitive/regulated code → private on-premises.

## Section: Ollama

Running AI models locally. Topics: transforming AI accessibility, local inference on consumer hardware, model quantisation, use cases for on-device models (privacy, offline work, low-latency), and how local models complement cloud models.

## Section: Terminal Agents

CLI entry points for agentic coding across tools. Topics: GitHub Copilot CLI (interactive and programmatic modes, approval flags, hooks, fleet mode), Claude Code CLI, Cursor agent CLI, Codex, and Devin Desktop — cloud vs local agents, MCP integration, and building agentic workflows in the terminal.

## Section: Security

Risks and best practices for secure AI-assisted coding. Topics: OWASP Top 10 risks in AI-generated code, prompt injection attacks, insecure code generation patterns, supply chain risks, secrets in context, and mitigation strategies. How to use AI to find security issues rather than introduce them.

## Section: Instructions

Teaching AI how you work — capability-first. Topics: project-wide vs scoped instructions, cross-tool `AGENTS.md` (portable instructions file — not the `.agents/` folder), tool-specific paths (`.cursor/rules`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`), system prompts, and instruction layering. Comparison matrices map concepts to each tool. For portable **skills** (not instructions), see Agents & Skills → Two Portable Layers.

## Section: Context

How AI processes and manages information. Topics: context window strategies, what to include and exclude, file references, keeping context clean, context poisoning risks, and techniques for long-running tasks (checkpoints, handoffs, summarisation).

## Section: Spec Driven Development

Making technical decisions explicit, reviewable, and executable. Topics: writing specifications before coding, using AI to validate specs, implementing from specs, the benefits of explicit assumptions, and how specs align teams and AI agents. Prevents costly rewrites from divergent assumptions.

## Section: Agents & Skills

Prompt files, custom agents, and agent skills. Topics: **Two Portable Layers** — `AGENTS.md` for cross-tool instructions and `.agents/skills/` for portable skills; `.agents/` is **skills-only** portability, not full cross-tool compatibility. Tool-native folders (`.cursor/`, `.claude/`, `.github/`, `.codex/`, `.devin/`) remain required for custom agents, rules, and MCP. Building reusable AI behaviours, the agent loop (LLM receives context → decides on tool call → tool executes → result fed back → repeat), tool use, skill composition, agent vs skill distinction, cross-tool comparison matrices, and Copilot subagents (runtime-only — no file path). For portable **instructions**, see Instructions → AGENTS.md.

**Facilitator gaps (as of mid-2026):**
- **Claude Code:** no native `.agents/skills/` — use `.claude/skills/` or `npx skills` symlink/copy
- **Cursor:** project `.agents/skills/` supported; global skills prefer `~/.cursor/skills/`
- **Devin Desktop:** reads `.agents/skills/` for compatibility; prefers `.devin/skills/` for writes
- **Copilot subagents:** runtime-only (unchanged from capability-first matrices)

## Section: Team Knowledge

Shared knowledge bases and team-wide AI configuration. Topics: Copilot Spaces (Copilot callout), APM compile, shared instruction repos, organisational knowledge management, versioning prompts and instructions, and onboarding new team members to AI workflows.

## Section: Evolution of the Programmer

The 8 stages from traditional developer to AI-native engineer:
- Stage 1: Zero or minimal AI use — traditional development workflow
- Stage 2: Coding agent in IDE with permission prompts — accepting/rejecting suggestions
- Stage 3: Broader agentic use — terminal agents, chat, multi-file edits
- Stage 4: Customised AI environment — custom instructions, MCP tools, personal workflows
- Stage 5: Spec-driven development — writing specs first, AI implements
- Stage 6: Agent orchestration — directing multiple agents on sub-tasks
- Stage 7: Continuous agentic workflows — background agents, async work, fleet mode
- Stage 8: Orchestrating 30+ parallel agents — fully AI-native engineering at scale

Covers how the developer role changes at each stage and what skills matter most.

## Section: Multi-Agent

Orchestrating multiple AI agents. Topics: five-step loop (define → delegate → parallelize → isolate → synthesize), hub-and-spoke delegation, git worktrees for isolation, orchestration matrices across tools, when multi-agent helps vs hurts, synthesis and merge discipline, and practical patterns for complex tasks.

## Section: Agent SDKs

Programmatic agent runtimes for applications. Topics: GitHub Copilot SDK (primary deep dive), Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents API, embedding agentic workflows in apps, and gaps where vendor SDKs are still maturing.

## Section: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

The universal standard for connecting AI to external systems. Topics: MCP servers, tools, resources, prompts, the client-server architecture, how to expose your own APIs to AI, existing MCP servers ecosystem, and building custom MCP tools.

## Section: What the Pros Use

Advanced patterns from the AI-native developer playbook. Topics: workflows, tooling stacks, and practices used by experienced AI developers. Voice-to-text (Wispr Flow), multi-model strategies, compound AI systems, and the meta-skill of tool selection.

## Section: Closing

Workshop summary, key takeaways, next steps for continued learning, and feedback.

---

## Key Concepts

- **Quantum State of Adoption** — AI is unique in that developers simultaneously exist across multiple stages of the technology adoption lifecycle, rather than moving through them sequentially
- **4D Fluency Framework** — Four competencies for AI collaboration: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence
- **Three AI Interaction Modes** — Augmentation (collaborative), Automation (task-specific), Agency (goal-directed)
- **Agent Loop** — LLM receives context → decides on tool call → tool executes → result fed back to LLM → repeat
- **Spec-Driven Development (SDD)** — Writing an explicit specification document before writing code; makes assumptions reviewable and prevents divergent implementations
- **Two Portable Layers** — `AGENTS.md` for instructions and `.agents/skills/` for skills; partial cross-tool portability (skills only). Custom agents, rules, and MCP stay tool-native
- **Agent vs Skill** — An agent defines what is demanded; a skill defines how to execute it. Skills live in tool-native paths or portable `.agents/skills/` where supported; agents can be chained
- **Pro Tool Stack principle** — Cheap/repetitive → fast local models (Ollama). Complex reasoning → frontier cloud (Claude, GPT, Gemini). Sensitive/regulated → private on-premises
